group.title: Economy and policy
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Cuts in public spending to reduce debt.
wrong: Austerity means the government spends much more.

words.meaning: The amount by which spending is more than income.
examples: The government has a large budget {deficit}.
wrong: A deficit is extra money left over after spending.

words.meaning: An amount that is more than what is needed.
wrong: A surplus means there isn’t enough.

words.meaning: Connected with government money and taxes.
wrong: Fiscal policy is about sports and games.

words.meaning: Connected with money, especially a country’s money supply.
wrong: Monetary policy is about schools, not money.

words.meaning: Something that encourages activity, like extra government spending.
wrong: A stimulus slows the economy on purpose.

words.meaning: To sell a public business to private owners.
wrong: They privatized the company by making the state own it.

words.meaning: To bring a private business under government control.
wrong: They nationalized the firm by selling it to private owners.

words.meaning: To remove government rules from an industry.
wrong: They deregulated the market by adding many new rules.

words.meaning: Complete control of a market by one company.
examples: The company had a {monopoly} on electricity.
wrong: A monopoly is a market with hundreds of rival firms.

words.meaning: A raw product that can be bought and sold, like oil or wheat.
wrong: A commodity is a service with nothing to trade.

words.meaning: The using of goods, energy or food.
wrong: Consumption means producing new goods.

words.meaning: Having a lot of money.
wrong: The area is affluent, so most people are poor.

words.meaning: The state of being successful and rich.
wrong: Prosperity is a time of great poverty.

words.meaning: The basic systems a country needs, such as roads and power.
wrong: Infrastructure means only luxury hotels.

words.meaning: An amount of money that must be paid, like a tax.
examples: The city added a {levy} on plastic bags.
wrong: A levy is a free gift from the government.

words.meaning: A system with many complicated rules and processes.
examples: Starting a business involves a lot of {bureaucracy}.
wrong: Bureaucracy means having no rules or forms at all.

words.meaning: The authority to act, given by voters.
examples: The election gave her a strong {mandate}.
wrong: A mandate is a loss of all authority.

words.meaning: The act of supplying something.
examples: The {provision} of clean water is vital.
wrong: Provision means taking supplies away.

words.meaning: An amount of something given for a purpose.
examples: Each school gets an {allocation} of funds.
wrong: An allocation is money that nobody receives.

words.meaning: Money paid regularly to someone after they retire.
wrong: A pension is money you pay to your first employer.

words.meaning: Money that you owe.
wrong: A debt is money that someone owes you as a gift.

words.meaning: The percentage charged for borrowing money.
wrong: An interest rate is how interesting a bank is.

words.meaning: The place where shares in companies are bought and sold.
wrong: The stock market is a shop for kitchen supplies.

words.meaning: A person who puts money into a business to make a profit.
examples: {Investors} lost money when the shares fell.
wrong: An investor is a person who never puts money into anything.

words.meaning: A person who starts a business and takes financial risks.
wrong: An entrepreneur avoids starting any business.

words.meaning: The process of economies and cultures becoming connected worldwide.
examples: {Globalization} has changed how goods are made.
wrong: Globalization means each country closes its borders.

words.meaning: A fall in business or economic activity.
wrong: A downturn is a period of fast growth.

words.meaning: A period of fast economic growth.
examples: There was a building {boom} in the city.
wrong: A boom is a time when business collapses.

words.meaning: A part of an economy, such as farming or banking.
wrong: A sector is the whole economy of every country.

words.meaning: A loan from a bank to buy a house.
examples: They took out a {mortgage} to buy their flat.
wrong: A mortgage is money the bank gives you for free.

words.meaning: Illegally not paying the tax you owe.
wrong: Tax evasion is paying more tax than you owe.

words.meaning: To pay part of the cost of something.
wrong: They subsidize the buses by charging extra.

words.meaning: Cheap enough for people to buy.
wrong: The flats are affordable, so nobody can pay for them.

words.meaning: Money left after paying taxes and bills.
wrong: Disposable income is money you must give to the government.

words.meaning: A wage high enough to pay for basic needs.
examples: Campaigners want a {living wage} for all workers.
wrong: A living wage is too low to buy food.

words.meaning: The amount of money needed for basic needs.
wrong: The cost of living is the price of one coffee.

words.meaning: Connected with trade, industry and money.
wrong: Economic growth is about the size of trees.

words.meaning: Using money, fuel or time carefully, without waste.
examples: This car is very {economical} on fuel.
wrong: The car is economical, so it wastes fuel.

words.meaning: Sharing wealth more equally across a society.
examples: Taxes can be a tool for {redistribution}.
wrong: Redistribution means giving all wealth to one person.
